name: Chiasmus: the mirror-image sentence
scope: The rhetorical figure where a phrase is repeated in reverse order. T1: the canonical example -- quote the closing line of John F. Kennedy's inaugural address, delivered on January 20, 1961: 'Ask not what your country can do for you -- ask what you can do for your country.' The two halves are mirror images: [country / you] -> [you / country]. Name that shape. Define CHIASMUS in-context as the pattern where the second half reverses the order of the first (from the Greek letter chi, X, whose two lines cross). T2: another canonical example -- Mark Twain's line, 'It is not the size of the dog in the fight, it is the size of the fight in the dog.' Identify the reversed pair (dog/fight -> fight/dog). T3: distinguish chiasmus from simple ANAPHORA (repetition at the START of clauses, like Churchill's 'we shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds') -- chiasmus REVERSES word order; anaphora only REPEATS an opening. T4: the Cormac McCarthy chiasmus from 'No Country for Old Men' (2005) -- 'You forget what you want to remember, and you remember what you want to forget.' Identify the reversed pair (forget/remember -> remember/forget). T5: subtle judgment -- given four quoted sentences (a chiasmus, an anaphora, an epistrophe, a parallel-structure list), identify which one is the chiasmus.
source: PRIMARY: Kennedy's inaugural address transcript (January 20, 1961); Mark Twain, 'This Was My Father', speech for the Republican Convention (July 4, 1904, common attribution); Cormac McCarthy, 'No Country for Old Men' (Alfred A. Knopf, 2005). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Chiasmus' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Greek-letter etymology, JFK/Twain canonical examples, and the anaphora/epistrophe/parallelism distinction. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: JFK's exact wording of the 'ask not' line before quoting; Twain attribution.
framing_note: Named-wordplay topic. Punchline via elegance: the sentence CLICKS when the reversal lands. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define CHIASMUS inline (>=30 chars) with the Greek-X etymology; T3 defines ANAPHORA the same way. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: quote the actual sentence in the stem, ask the kid to NAME the shape or IDENTIFY the reversed pair. DISTRACTOR POOL: other rhetorical figures (anaphora, epistrophe, anadiplosis, parallelism, antithesis, alliteration). CHOICE PARITY: if the answer is a device name, all four choices are device names of similar length.
history_overlap: LITERATURE owns Cormac McCarthy as a novelist; HISTORY owns JFK's presidency as political fact -- here both are cited only as sources of the grammatical example.

name: Zeugma and syllepsis: one verb, incompatible objects
scope: The rhetorical figure where a single verb governs two or more objects in incompatible senses. T1: the canonical Flanders-and-Swann line (Michael Flanders and Donald Swann, British comic songwriters, mid-20th century) -- 'She lowered her standards by raising her glass, her courage, her eyes, and his hopes.' One verb (raising) is stretched across four objects that each take it in a slightly different sense (a glass literally, courage figuratively, eyes toward someone, hopes emotionally). Name that shape. Define ZEUGMA in-context as one verb governing multiple objects. T2: the classic Alexander Pope line from 'The Rape of the Lock' (1712) -- 'Or stain her honour, or her new brocade.' One verb (stain) governs a moral object (honour) and a literal object (a dress) at the same time. T3: distinguish ZEUGMA (broad term for the sharing) from SYLLEPSIS (the version where the shared verb fits each object grammatically but shifts MEANING between them). Most modern usage lumps them together, but strict rhetoric splits them. T4: identify a zeugma in a set of four quoted sentences -- one has the shared-verb-shifting-meaning pattern, the others use parallelism, chiasmus, or straightforward metaphor. T5: judgment case -- 'She broke his heart and his favorite vase.' Argue whether this is zeugma (yes: BROKE means one thing physically and one thing emotionally) or just an ordinary compound object (no: 'broke' is loose enough that both readings are fine). The punchline IS the ambiguity.
source: PRIMARY: Michael Flanders and Donald Swann, 'Have Some Madeira, M'Dear' (song, 1957); Alexander Pope, 'The Rape of the Lock' Canto II line 107 (1712 revised 1714). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Zeugma and syllepsis' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Pope example, the Flanders-Swann example, and the strict-vs-loose zeugma/syllepsis distinction. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Pope's exact wording of the 'stain her honour' line.
framing_note: Named-wordplay topic. Punchline via the audible click of the same verb doing two different jobs. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define ZEUGMA inline; T3 defines SYLLEPSIS. Kid-safe examples only -- Flanders/Swann and Pope are both in the safe canon. DISTRACTOR POOL: chiasmus, anaphora, parallelism, metaphor, pun. CHOICE PARITY across corrected sentences or device-name choices.

name: Anaphora and epistrophe: repetition at the start, repetition at the end
scope: The two mirror-image repetition figures. T1: quote the most famous ANAPHORA in English -- Winston Churchill in the House of Commons on June 4, 1940: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender.' The phrase 'we shall fight' STARTS each clause. Define ANAPHORA in-context as the repetition of the same word or phrase at the BEGINNING of successive clauses. T2: quote another anaphora -- Martin Luther King Jr., Lincoln Memorial, August 28, 1963: 'I have a dream that one day ... I have a dream that ... I have a dream today.' Identify the repeated opener. T3: define the mirror figure -- EPISTROPHE, the repetition at the END of successive clauses. Quote Lincoln's Gettysburg Address (November 19, 1863): 'government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.' The phrase 'the people' ENDS each of the three governing phrases. T4: given a quoted passage, identify whether it uses anaphora (start-repetition), epistrophe (end-repetition), or symploce (both at once). T5: subtle judgment -- distinguish anaphora from ANADIPLOSIS (repetition that carries the LAST word of one clause to the FIRST word of the next, e.g. 'Fear leads to anger. Anger leads to hate. Hate leads to suffering.' -- Yoda in 'The Phantom Menace', 1999). Anaphora repeats openers across clauses; anadiplosis links clause-end to next-clause-start.
source: PRIMARY: Winston Churchill, 'We Shall Fight on the Beaches' speech, House of Commons (June 4, 1940); Martin Luther King Jr., 'I Have a Dream' speech (August 28, 1963); Abraham Lincoln, Gettysburg Address (November 19, 1863). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Anaphora (rhetoric)' and 'Epistrophe' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the definitions and the Churchill/King/Lincoln canonical examples; also 'Anadiplosis' for the Yoda-line contrast. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Churchill's exact wording of the 'we shall fight' passage; Lincoln's exact 'of/by/for the people'.
framing_note: Two rhetorical figures taught together because they mirror each other. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1, T3, T5: define ANAPHORA, EPISTROPHE, and ANADIPLOSIS inline. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: quote the actual passage, then ask which figure is present. DISTRACTOR POOL: chiasmus, parallelism, alliteration, symploce, anadiplosis. Historical/political quotes are FINE as EXAMPLES of the device (per lane-borders in the voice rule).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Churchill's war leadership, MLK's civil-rights leadership, and Lincoln's presidency as political fact -- here each is cited only as the source of the grammatical example.

name: Malapropism: Mrs. Malaprop and the wrong word for the right sound
scope: The comic error where a speaker substitutes a similar-sounding word with a very different meaning. T1: the canonical example from the character the whole device is named after -- Mrs. Malaprop, in Richard Brinsley Sheridan's play 'The Rivals' (first performed at Covent Garden, London, January 17, 1775): 'He is the very PINEAPPLE of politeness!' (she meant PINNACLE). Name that error. Define MALAPROPISM in-context as the use of a wrong word that sounds similar to the intended one, usually producing a laugh. T2: another Mrs. Malaprop line from the same play -- 'She is as headstrong as an ALLEGORY on the banks of the Nile' (she meant ALLIGATOR). Identify the intended word. T3: the term itself comes from a French phrase -- 'mal a propos', meaning 'badly for the purpose' or 'inappropriately.' Sheridan named the character Malaprop as a joke; the character's name gave English the noun for the error. T4: the modern master of the malapropism -- baseball catcher Yogi Berra (1925-2015), famous for lines like 'Texas has a lot of electrical votes' (electoral) and 'He must have made that before he died' (about a Steve McQueen movie). Identify which of four quoted lines is a Yogi-Berra-style malapropism vs a straight metaphor, mixed metaphor, or pun. T5: distinguish MALAPROPISM (wrong-word substitution) from EGGCORN (a systematic misinterpretation that MAKES a kind of sense, like 'for all intensive purposes' for 'for all intents and purposes') and SPOONERISM (swapped sounds within or across words). All three are speech errors; the punchline is which category the mistake falls into.
source: PRIMARY: Richard Brinsley Sheridan, 'The Rivals' (Act III scene III for the pineapple line; Act III scene III for the allegory line; first performed at Covent Garden Theatre, London, January 17, 1775). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Malapropism' and 'Mrs. Malaprop' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the 'mal a propos' etymology, the Sheridan attribution, Yogi Berra examples, and the malapropism/eggcorn/spoonerism distinction; 'Yogi Berra' for the baseball-catcher biography and the electoral-votes line.
framing_note: Named-wordplay topic; comic-error family. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define MALAPROPISM inline; T5 defines EGGCORN and SPOONERISM. Punny-dad voice throughout -- Mrs. Malaprop and Yogi Berra are safe-canon comic figures. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: quote the wrong line, ask the kid to spot the intended word or name the error type. DISTRACTOR POOL: other speech-error categories (spoonerism, eggcorn, mondegreen, tongue-twister). Kid-safe throughout.
history_overlap: LITERATURE owns 'The Rivals' as a play; here it is cited only as the source of the malapropism etymology.

name: Spoonerism: the Reverend who swapped his sounds
scope: The speech error where the opening sounds of two words are swapped. T1: the canonical example attributed to the man the device is named after -- Reverend William Archibald Spooner (1844-1930), Warden of New College, Oxford. He reportedly told a student: 'You have TASTED THE WHOLE WORM' -- he meant WASTED THE WHOLE TERM. Name that error. Define SPOONERISM in-context as a slip in which the opening consonants (or syllables) of two words are exchanged. T2: another spoonerism attributed to Spooner -- 'You have HISSED all my MYSTERY lectures' (he meant MISSED my HISTORY lectures). Identify the intended pair. T3: another apocryphal Spooner line -- 'a BLUSHING CROW' for 'a CRUSHING BLOW.' Note that many spoonerisms attributed to Spooner are LATER inventions; he probably said only a handful of them, but the pattern was so funny his name stuck to all of them. T4: distinguish a SPOONERISM (swapped sounds between two words) from a MALAPROPISM (wrong word substituted for a similar-sounding one) and a TONGUE-TWISTER (a phrase deliberately hard to say fast). Given four quoted errors, pick the spoonerism. T5: the deliberate-spoonerism payoff -- W.C. Fields's joke 'I'd rather have a bottle in front of me than a frontal lobotomy' is a chiasmic spoonerism-style pun on 'bottle in front' / 'frontal lobotomy'. Identify what makes it a spoonerism-shape rather than a simple pun.
source: PRIMARY: biographical entry for William Archibald Spooner in the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography; Bill Bryson, 'Mother Tongue: English and How It Got That Way' (William Morrow, 1990) for the Spooner-mostly-apocryphal note. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Spoonerism' and 'William Archibald Spooner' (browser, 2026-09-05) for Spooner's 1844-1930 dates, his Wardenship of New College Oxford, and the note that many attributed lines are later inventions.
framing_note: Named-wordplay topic; comic-error family paired with the malapropism topic. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define SPOONERISM inline. Kid-safe throughout. ACCURACY RAIL: most attributed Spoonerisms are apocryphal -- state this in T3 rather than presenting all lines as historical. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: quote the wrong line, ask the kid to reconstruct the intended one or name the error type. DISTRACTOR POOL: malapropism, eggcorn, tongue-twister, pun.

name: Portmanteau: Lewis Carroll's word-suitcases
scope: The word formed by blending two others. T1: the term itself comes from a passage in Lewis Carroll's 'Through the Looking-Glass' (1871), where Humpty Dumpty explains to Alice the nonsense words of the poem 'Jabberwocky': 'You see, it's like a PORTMANTEAU -- there are two meanings packed up into one word.' A portmanteau was an old-fashioned travel case that opened into two hinged compartments. Define PORTMANTEAU in-context as a word formed by blending two others. T2: everyday examples -- BRUNCH (breakfast + lunch), SMOG (smoke + fog), MOTEL (motor + hotel), SPORK (spoon + fork). Identify the two source words of a given portmanteau. T3: modern-tech examples -- EMOTICON (emotion + icon), PODCAST (iPod + broadcast), SITCOM (situation + comedy), INFOMERCIAL (information + commercial). Match blends to sources. T4: Lewis Carroll's own portmanteaus from 'Jabberwocky' -- SLITHY (slimy + lithe), CHORTLE (chuckle + snort), MIMSY (miserable + flimsy). CHORTLE and GALUMPHING actually entered ordinary English from that one nonsense poem. Identify which everyday English words came from Carroll. T5: distinguish a PORTMANTEAU (two words BLENDED, sharing sounds -- brunch, smog) from a COMPOUND WORD (two words STUCK together, both intact -- bookshelf, sunflower) and an ACRONYM (initials taken from a phrase -- NASA, radar). Categorize four given words.
source: PRIMARY: Lewis Carroll, 'Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There' (Macmillan, 1871), Chapter VI 'Humpty Dumpty'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Portmanteau' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Carroll etymology, the standard examples (brunch, smog, motel), and the Jabberwocky-coinages that entered English (chortle, galumphing). Oxford English Dictionary entries for 'chortle' (first attested 1871, Carroll) and 'galumphing' (first attested 1871, Carroll).
framing_note: Named-wordplay topic with etymology twist. Punchline via the Humpty-Dumpty image of a suitcase with two hinged halves. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define PORTMANTEAU inline with the suitcase etymology; T5 defines COMPOUND WORD and ACRONYM. Kid-safe throughout. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: give the blend, ask for the sources; or give the sources, ask for the blend. DISTRACTOR POOL: compound words, acronyms, backronyms, eponyms.
history_overlap: LITERATURE owns Carroll's novels; here they are cited only as the source of the term and the coinages.

name: Backronym: the acronym invented AFTER the word
scope: The retroactive acronym -- an existing word later given an invented initials-based explanation. T1: the term BACKRONYM was itself coined by Meredith G. Williams in a 1983 Washington Post reader contest, formed as a portmanteau of BACK + ACRONYM. Define BACKRONYM in-context as a phrase invented to fit an existing word's letters, treating them as if they had been an acronym all along. T2: the SOS example -- 'Save Our Souls' and 'Save Our Ship' are backronyms; the maritime distress signal SOS was actually chosen in 1906 simply because ... ... ... (three dots, three dashes, three dots) is unmistakable in Morse code and easy to send under stress. The letters were picked for the Morse, not for any phrase. T3: the TIP example -- the folk-etymology story that TIP means 'To Insure Promptness' is a backronym; the word TIP has meant a small gratuity since at least the 1600s, well before the phrase was invented to explain it. T4: given four common words with initials-based folk explanations (POSH -- 'Port Out, Starboard Home', GOLF -- 'Gentlemen Only, Ladies Forbidden', FUCK -- one of several sanitized origin myths, NEWS -- 'North East West South'), identify which are backronyms rather than true acronymic origins. All four in that list are backronyms; the real origins are older and unrelated. T5: distinguish a BACKRONYM (word predates the initials story) from a real ACRONYM (initials predate the pronounceable word: NASA, LASER, RADAR, SCUBA) and from an INITIALISM (initials spoken as separate letters: FBI, HTML, DNA). Categorize four given words.
source: PRIMARY: Meredith G. Williams, winning entry, Washington Post 'Style Invitational' neologism contest (1983); Oxford English Dictionary entries for 'tip', 'posh', 'golf', 'news' (all pre-dating the initials-based folk stories). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Backronym' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the term's 1983 Williams coinage, SOS-as-Morse-choice, tip/posh/golf folk-etymology debunkings, and the acronym/initialism/backronym distinction. Bill Bryson, 'Mother Tongue' (1990) for the general folk-etymology-of-English pattern.
framing_note: Named-wordplay topic + folk-etymology debunking. Punchline via the reveal that a familiar 'obviously an acronym' story is actually invented after the fact. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define BACKRONYM inline. Kid-safe examples only (the sanitized common-word case at T4 uses NEWS/POSH/GOLF; the crude one is mentioned in the source note but NOT written into a rung). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: give the word + the folk-etymology, ask whether it is a backronym. DISTRACTOR POOL: acronym, initialism, portmanteau, eponym.

name: Contronym: the word that means its own opposite
scope: The bizarre category of English words that carry two opposite meanings at once. T1: the canonical example -- CLEAVE can mean 'to split apart' (a cleaver cleaves meat in two) OR 'to cling to' (a husband cleaves to his wife, in the wedding vow). Same word; opposite senses. Define CONTRONYM in-context as a word that has two opposite meanings, also called an auto-antonym or a Janus word (after the two-faced Roman god who looked in opposite directions). T2: another canonical example -- SANCTION can mean 'to permit or approve' (the boss sanctioned the plan) OR 'to punish' (economic sanctions were imposed). The context alone tells you which sense is meant. T3: the DUST example -- to DUST can mean 'to remove particles' (I dusted the shelf) OR 'to add particles' (the baker dusted the pastry with sugar). Give a quoted sentence, identify which sense is in play. T4: the OVERSIGHT example -- OVERSIGHT can mean 'careful supervision' (the committee provides oversight of the project) OR 'a careless mistake' (that was an oversight on my part). Two dictionary entries, both alive today. Identify the opposite-meaning pair in each of four sentences. T5: more contronyms -- SCREEN (to hide, or to display), TRIM (to add decoration to, or to cut away from), BOUND (heading toward, or tied up unable to move), FAST (moving quickly, or stuck firmly in place -- 'hold fast'). Given a paragraph, identify each contronym and specify which of its two opposite meanings is in force.
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary entries for 'cleave', 'sanction', 'dust', 'oversight', 'screen', 'trim', 'bound', 'fast'. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Auto-antonym' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the term contronym/auto-antonym/Janus-word, the two-faced-Roman-god etymology, and the canonical example list.
framing_note: Named-wordplay topic. Punchline via the reveal that a single familiar word can mean its own opposite. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define CONTRONYM inline with the Janus etymology. Kid-safe examples throughout. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: give a quoted sentence, ask which sense of the word is in play or ask the kid to identify the contronym in the sentence. DISTRACTOR POOL: synonym, antonym, homophone, homograph.

name: Buffalo buffalo: the sentence that uses one word eight ways
scope: The famous grammatical brain-teaser. T1: warm-up rung -- 'Fish fish fish.' A grammatical English sentence using one word three times. Parsed: [Fish that other fish fish] fish (verb: to fish). Meaning: fish that other fish catch, themselves catch things. Introduce the trick -- the word BUFFALO likewise has three meanings: BUFFALO (with a capital B, the city in New York state), buffalo (the animal, plural same as singular), and buffalo (a verb meaning 'to bully' or 'to intimidate,' from 19th-century American slang). T2: the four-word version -- 'Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo.' Parsed: [buffalo (animals) from Buffalo (the city)] buffalo (verb: bully) buffalo (other animals). Meaning: New York State buffalo bully other buffalo. T3: the famous eight-word canonical sentence popularized by William J. Rapaport (State University of New York at Buffalo, 1972 lecture): 'Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo.' Parsed: [Buffalo buffalo (bison from Buffalo, NY) whom Buffalo buffalo (other Buffalo bison) buffalo (bully)] buffalo (verb: bully) Buffalo buffalo (still other Buffalo bison). Every word is spelled the same, but they take three different grammatical roles. T4: distinguish the three uses in a given rendering -- pick which BUFFALO is the proper noun (city), which is the common noun (animal), which is the verb (bully). T5: the general principle -- English is full of words that can serve as noun, verb, and modifier ('rock', 'saw', 'plant', 'run'), but BUFFALO is unusual because a single spelling can plausibly fill EVERY slot in a sentence eight words long. Identify which of four candidate 'trick' sentences works the same way ('James while John had had had had had had had had had had had a better effect on the teacher' is the other famous one, from a 1972 paper).
source: PRIMARY: William J. Rapaport, 'A History of the Sentence Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo' (SUNY Buffalo departmental note, 1972; revised online 1994); Steven Pinker, 'The Language Instinct' (William Morrow, 1994), Chapter 4 for the wider tree-diagram context. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Rapaport attribution, the three-meaning breakdown, the escalating 3-word / 4-word / 8-word ladder, and the James-had-had-had had-had counterpart sentence.
framing_note: Named-wordplay topic; the bank's flagship T5 puzzle. Punchline via the reveal that the whole sentence is one word repeated. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define the three senses of BUFFALO inline. ACCURACY RAIL: attribution goes to Rapaport (1972); Pinker popularized it but did not coin it. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: at each rung, quote the sentence, ask the kid to identify which BUFFALO is which grammatical role. DISTRACTOR POOL: chiasmus, garden-path sentence, tongue-twister, homograph. This ladder builds tier by tier (3 words -> 4 words -> 8 words) rather than mixing tiers of unrelated punchlines.

name: Time flies like an arrow: the parsing-ambiguity pun
scope: The famous two-part sentence that turns on a shift in parsing. T1: the canonical whole -- 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana.' The first half reads normally (time passes swiftly, as an arrow flies). The second half re-parses every word -- FRUIT FLIES is now a noun-noun compound (the little insects, Drosophila), LIKE is now a verb (to enjoy), and A BANANA is the object of that verb. Same-shape sentence; totally different parse. Name what the pun turns on. T2: identify the shifted parts of speech -- in 'Time flies like an arrow', TIME is a noun and FLIES is a verb; in 'fruit flies like a banana', FRUIT FLIES together are a noun-phrase and LIKE is the verb. T3: the sentence is often attributed to Groucho Marx -- but the earliest documented print use appears in a 1966 paper by Anthony Oettinger (Harvard computational linguist), used as an example of the difficulty of automatic parsing. Attribution rail: 'variously attributed to Groucho Marx, likely apocryphal; documented in print by Oettinger 1966'. T4: distinguish this from a garden-path sentence -- both involve mid-sentence re-parsing, but the time-flies pun involves TWO parallel sentences that share a shape, while a garden-path sentence forces the reader to back up MID-SENTENCE (like 'The horse raced past the barn fell'). T5: given four quoted lines, identify which is a parsing-ambiguity pun (two-clause shift), which is a garden-path (mid-clause reparse), which is a straight pun on word meaning, and which is a spoonerism. The famous 'Fruit flies like a banana' is the parsing pun; 'The complex houses married soldiers' is the garden-path.
source: PRIMARY: Anthony G. Oettinger, 'The Uses of Computers in Science', Scientific American (September 1966), for the earliest documented parsing-example use of the sentence. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the attribution history (Groucho Marx apocryphal; Oettinger 1966 documented) and the parsing-vs-garden-path distinction. Steven Pinker, 'The Language Instinct' (1994) for the wider tree-diagram context.
framing_note: Named-wordplay topic; parsing-ambiguity family. Punchline via the sudden second-half re-parse. Vocab-teaching invariant: 'noun-noun compound' is defined inline at T2. ACCURACY RAIL: attribute to Oettinger 1966 documented, note Groucho Marx as apocryphal. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: quote the sentence, ask the kid to identify what changes between the two halves. DISTRACTOR POOL: garden-path sentence, straight pun, spoonerism, malapropism.

name: Palindromes: sentences that read the same backwards
scope: Words and sentences that read identically forward and backward. T1: the simplest examples -- single words like RACECAR, LEVEL, KAYAK, and NOON read the same left-to-right and right-to-left. Define PALINDROME in-context as a word, phrase, or sentence that reads the same in both directions (from Greek 'palin dromos', 'running back'). T2: the classic short-sentence palindromes -- 'Madam, I'm Adam' (spaces and punctuation ignored) and 'Never odd or even' and 'A Toyota's a Toyota.' Identify which of four candidate sentences is truly a palindrome and which merely LOOKS like one. T3: the most famous English palindrome, composed by British puzzler Leigh Mercer and published in Notes and Queries in 1948: 'A man, a plan, a canal -- Panama.' Refers to the Panama Canal, opened in 1914. T4: given a candidate long-sentence palindrome, verify or refute it by reading right-to-left. Napoleon's supposed lament 'Able was I ere I saw Elba' (referring to his 1814 exile to the island of Elba) is a real palindrome and is often attributed to him -- but the palindrome was actually composed by a 19th-century puzzler in an English magazine, NOT by Napoleon himself. Attribution rail: 'often attributed to Napoleon; actually a later English composition'. T5: distinguish PALINDROMES (same forward and backward) from ANAGRAMS (letters rearranged) and PANGRAMS (uses every letter). Given four sentences, categorize each. Punchline: 'Was it a car or a cat I saw?' is a palindrome; 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' is a pangram; 'William Shakespeare -> I am a weakish speller' is an anagram.
source: PRIMARY: Leigh Mercer, 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama' in Notes and Queries (1948). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Palindrome' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Greek 'palin dromos' etymology, the Mercer 1948 attribution for the Panama palindrome, and the note that 'Able was I ere I saw Elba' is a later English composition not authored by Napoleon.
framing_note: Named-wordplay topic with a light etymology thread. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define PALINDROME inline with the Greek etymology; T5 defines ANAGRAM and PANGRAM. Punchline via the click of reading a sentence backward and getting the same words. ACCURACY RAIL: the Elba palindrome is NOT actually Napoleon; the Panama palindrome IS Leigh Mercer 1948. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: quote the candidate sentence, ask whether it is a palindrome (or which type of wordplay it is). DISTRACTOR POOL: anagram, pangram, chiasmus, portmanteau.

name: Pangram and anagram: every letter, or the letters rearranged
scope: The two letter-based word games often confused with palindromes. T1: PANGRAM -- a sentence that uses every letter of the alphabet at least once. The canonical English pangram, used since the late 1800s by typewriter and typography demonstrations, is 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.' Count the alphabet in that sentence; every letter A-Z appears. Define PANGRAM in-context as a sentence using every letter of the alphabet. T2: shorter (harder!) pangrams -- 'Pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs' (32 letters), 'Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow' (29 letters). Identify which of four sentences is a pangram by checking whether all 26 letters appear. T3: ANAGRAM -- a word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of another. Define ANAGRAM in-context. The most famous English anagram game: rearrange 'William Shakespeare' to get 'I am a weakish speller' (all letters accounted for). T4: everyday anagrams -- LISTEN -> SILENT; DEBIT CARD -> BAD CREDIT; ELEVEN PLUS TWO -> TWELVE PLUS ONE (same letters, same sum). Given a target word, pick which of four options is a true anagram (using exactly its letters, no more, no less). T5: distinguish PANGRAM (every letter used) from ANAGRAM (letters rearranged) from PALINDROME (letters reverse-symmetric). Given four short sentences, categorize each. Punchline: 'The quick brown fox' is a pangram, 'I am a weakish speller' is an anagram, 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama' is a palindrome, and 'Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo' is a syntactic ambiguity, not any of the three letter-games.
source: PRIMARY: Merriam-Webster's Dictionary entries for 'pangram' and 'anagram'; the fox-jumps-lazy-dog pangram traces to typewriter-typing training manuals (in Michigan School Moderator, 1885). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Pangram' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the fox-pangram origin and shorter alternatives; 'Anagram' for the Shakespeare/listen-silent classics.
framing_note: Named-wordplay topic paired with the palindrome ladder. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1 and T3: define PANGRAM and ANAGRAM inline. Punchline via the recognition that these three letter-games (pangram, anagram, palindrome) are constantly confused but each does one specific thing. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: give a candidate sentence or word pair, ask the kid to identify which game it is. DISTRACTOR POOL: palindrome, portmanteau, contronym, alliteration.

name: Eponyms: sandwiches, boycotts, and silhouettes
scope: Common English words that come from real people's names. T1: SANDWICH -- named for John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich (1718-1792), a British nobleman who, according to a story first told by a contemporary, ordered meat between two pieces of bread so he could keep gambling at cards without stopping to eat with a knife and fork. The bread-and-filling snack took his title. Define EPONYM in-context as a common word formed from a person's name. T2: BOYCOTT -- from Captain Charles Boycott (1832-1897), an English land agent in County Mayo, Ireland. In 1880, during the Irish Land War, local tenants and workers refused to serve him or work his estate; his name became the verb for that collective refusal to deal with someone. T3: SILHOUETTE -- from Etienne de Silhouette (1709-1767), a French finance minister famous for cheapness during the Seven Years' War. Cut-paper profile portraits were nicknamed 'a la silhouette' because they were the cheapest way to get someone's likeness; his name stuck to the shape. T4: more eponyms -- CARDIGAN (from the 7th Earl of Cardigan, James Brudenell, who wore knitted waistcoats during the 1854 Crimean War), NICOTINE (from Jean Nicot, the French ambassador who sent tobacco seeds to Paris in 1560), MESMERIZE (from Franz Mesmer, 1734-1815, the German physician of 'animal magnetism'). Match word to person. T5: distinguish TRUE EPONYMS (word IS the person's name, or clearly derived) from BACKRONYMS (a phrase invented AFTER the word to fit its letters) and from FOLK ETYMOLOGY (a false origin story attached to a word whose real origin is different). Given four words with origin stories, categorize each.
source: PRIMARY: Oxford English Dictionary entries for 'sandwich' (first attested 1762), 'boycott' (first attested 1880), 'silhouette' (first attested 1798), 'cardigan' (first attested 1868), 'nicotine' (first attested 1819), 'mesmerize' (first attested 1829). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Eponym', 'John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich', 'Charles Boycott', 'Etienne de Silhouette', 'James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan', 'Jean Nicot' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the biographical facts and the earliest citations.
framing_note: Named-wordplay + etymology topic. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define EPONYM inline. Punchline via the reveal that a common word is literally a person's name. Kid-safe throughout (no crude eponyms). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: give the word, ask for the person; or give the person's story, ask for the word. DISTRACTOR POOL: backronym, portmanteau, folk etymology, borrowing from another language.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the biographies of Sandwich, Boycott, Silhouette, Cardigan, Nicot, Mesmer as historical figures -- here each is cited only as the source of an English word.

name: Onomatopoeia: words that sound like what they mean
scope: The category of words that imitate the sound they describe. T1: everyday examples -- BUZZ (like a bee), HISS (like a snake), MEOW (like a cat), MOO (like a cow), PLOP (like something small hitting water). Say them aloud; the sound of the word IS the sound of the thing. Define ONOMATOPOEIA in-context as a word whose sound imitates its meaning (from Greek 'onoma' name + 'poiein' to make -- literally 'name-making'). T2: comic-book onomatopoeia -- POW, BAM, ZAP, WHACK, KABOOM. Not every made-up sound-word is a real English word, but many of the classic comic-book ones (BAM, POW, ZAP) appear in ordinary dictionaries now. Identify which of four given words is standard onomatopoeia vs a nonce word. T3: bird names as onomatopoeia -- CUCKOO, WHIPPOORWILL, CHICKADEE, KILLDEER, BOBOLINK. Each bird is named for the sound of its call. Identify which of four given bird names is a sound-imitation. T4: onomatopoeia varies by LANGUAGE. In English a dog says 'woof' or 'bow-wow'; in Japanese, 'wan-wan'; in Korean, 'meong-meong'; in Turkish, 'hev-hev'; in Russian, 'gav-gav'. In English a rooster says 'cock-a-doodle-doo'; in Japanese, 'kokekokko'; in French, 'cocorico'. The sounds are real; the words differ. Identify a claim about cross-language onomatopoeia. T5: distinguish ONOMATOPOEIA (word imitates a sound) from ALLITERATION (words start with the same sound: 'she sells seashells by the sea shore') and from ASSONANCE (repeated vowel sounds inside words: 'the rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain'). Given four quoted lines, categorize each.
source: PRIMARY: Oxford English Dictionary entries for 'onomatopoeia' (Greek etymology), 'cuckoo', 'whippoorwill', 'chickadee'; standard English/Japanese/French/Russian dictionaries for the cross-language dog and rooster sounds. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Onomatopoeia' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the Greek etymology, the cross-language animal-sound comparisons, and the alliteration/assonance distinction.
framing_note: Named-wordplay topic; child-friendly. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define ONOMATOPOEIA inline with the Greek 'name-making' etymology; T5 defines ALLITERATION and ASSONANCE. Punchline via the reveal that the same real-world sound gets different word-shapes in different languages. Kid-safe throughout (animals, comic books, weather). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: give the word, ask what it imitates; or give the sound-source, ask for the word. DISTRACTOR POOL: alliteration, assonance, portmanteau, eponym.

name: Metaphor vs simile: with or without LIKE / AS
scope: The strict distinction that half the internet gets wrong. T1: the canonical wrong-version -- someone says 'That was a great simile' about a line like 'My love is a red, red rose.' It is not a simile; it is a METAPHOR. Define both in-context: SIMILE compares two things using the words LIKE or AS ('my love is LIKE a red, red rose'); METAPHOR compares two things DIRECTLY, saying one IS the other ('my love IS a red, red rose'). The presence or absence of LIKE/AS is the whole difference. T2: identify each -- 'Life is a highway' (metaphor -- IS), 'Life is like a box of chocolates' (simile -- LIKE), 'She was as brave as a lion' (simile -- AS), 'He is a lion in battle' (metaphor -- IS). Sort four quoted sentences into metaphor vs simile. T3: Robert Burns's 1794 poem 'A Red, Red Rose' opens 'O my Luve is like a red, red rose that's newly sprung in June.' Because Burns wrote LIKE, it is a simile -- despite generations of readers half-remembering it as a metaphor. Accuracy note: quote the original correctly. T4: an EXTENDED METAPHOR (also called a CONCEIT) is a metaphor stretched across many sentences or a whole poem or paragraph. Shakespeare's 'All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players' (As You Like It, Act II Scene VII, c. 1600) is an extended metaphor: the world IS a stage; people ARE actors; life has ACTS; each of us plays MANY PARTS. Identify what makes it extended rather than a single metaphor. T5: distinguish SIMILE, METAPHOR, EXTENDED METAPHOR, and ANALOGY. ANALOGY explains an unfamiliar thing by structural comparison to a familiar one (an atom is like a solar system -- nucleus/sun in the middle, electrons/planets orbiting around); it can be phrased as either a simile or a metaphor. Given four passages, identify which is which.
source: PRIMARY: Robert Burns, 'A Red, Red Rose' (Scots Musical Museum, 1794); William Shakespeare, 'As You Like It', Act II Scene VII, lines 139-166 (first published in the 1623 First Folio, written c. 1599-1600). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Simile', 'Metaphor', 'Extended metaphor' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the like/as distinction, the Burns and Shakespeare canonical extended-metaphor examples, and the analogy contrast. Standard style-guide entries (Merriam-Webster, Chicago 5.257-5.259).
framing_note: Register-and-recognition topic. Punchline via correcting a common casual error ('great simile' for a metaphor). Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define SIMILE and METAPHOR inline; T4 defines EXTENDED METAPHOR; T5 defines ANALOGY. ACCURACY RAIL: Burns's 'red rose' line is a simile, NOT a metaphor -- state this clearly. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: quote the actual line, ask which figure it is. DISTRACTOR POOL: analogy, personification, hyperbole, allusion.
history_overlap: LITERATURE owns Burns's poetry and Shakespeare's plays as literary works; here each is cited only as the source of the grammatical example.

name: Semantic shift: nice used to mean foolish
scope: The category of English words whose meaning has drifted, sometimes to the opposite of the original. T1: NICE. In Middle English (c. 1300), NICE meant 'foolish, silly, or ignorant', from Latin 'nescius' meaning 'not knowing.' Over roughly six centuries, it drifted from 'foolish' to 'shy' to 'refined' to 'kind' -- almost the opposite of where it started. Define SEMANTIC SHIFT in-context as the change in a word's meaning over time. T2: AWFUL. Originally meant 'full of awe' -- awe-inspiring, majestic, worthy of reverence. God was 'awful' in the 1500s in a wholly positive sense. Today AWFUL means bad, and 'awesome' has taken over the positive meaning. Same root; opposite outcome. Identify the earlier meaning of a given word. T3: SILLY. In Old English (saelig, c. 900) meant 'blessed, happy, holy' -- the same Germanic root as German 'selig' (blessed). It slid through 'innocent' to 'defenseless' to 'foolish', where it landed by around 1600. Identify a Middle-English or Old-English earlier meaning. T4: GIRL. In Middle English (c. 1300), 'girl' meant 'a young person of either sex' -- a boy could be called a girl. The word narrowed to 'young female' by the 1500s. Bill Bryson's 'Mother Tongue' (1990) uses this as a favourite example of semantic NARROWING (a word whose meaning shrinks over time). Identify which of four given words has narrowed vs widened vs shifted-opposite. T5: distinguish SEMANTIC NARROWING (meat = any food -> flesh food), SEMANTIC WIDENING (dog = a specific breed -> all dogs; holiday = holy day -> any day off), SEMANTIC AMELIORATION (knight = boy servant -> noble warrior), and SEMANTIC PEJORATION (silly = blessed -> foolish; villain = farm worker -> criminal). Given four word-history claims, categorize each. Etymology fact rail: every claim in this ladder is cited from the Oxford English Dictionary or Bryson's 'Mother Tongue' (1990).
source: PRIMARY: Oxford English Dictionary entries for 'nice' (from Latin nescius, first attested with 'foolish' sense c. 1290), 'awful' (from awe + -ful, 'full of awe' first attested c. 1300), 'silly' (from Old English saelig, first attested with 'foolish' sense 1548), 'girl' (Middle English gyrle, either sex c. 1300), 'meat', 'knight', 'villain'. CONSULTED: Bill Bryson, 'Mother Tongue: English and How It Got That Way' (William Morrow, 1990) for the girl/silly/nice examples and the narrowing/widening framework. Grokipedia 'Semantic change' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the amelioration/pejoration/narrowing/widening taxonomy.
framing_note: Etymology topic. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define SEMANTIC SHIFT inline; T5 defines NARROWING/WIDENING/AMELIORATION/PEJORATION. Punchline via the reveal that a familiar everyday word once meant its opposite. Kid-safe throughout (nice, awful, silly, girl -- no crude examples). ACCURACY RAIL: every dating and every earlier meaning traces to the OED; state that in the source. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: give the modern word, ask the earlier meaning; or give the earlier meaning, ask what the word became. DISTRACTOR POOL: false etymologies (folk etymology), portmanteau, backronym.

name: False friends: eventually and eventualmente
scope: Word pairs across languages that LOOK identical but MEAN different things. T1: the canonical case -- English EVENTUALLY means 'at some later point, finally, in the end' (I'll get to it eventually). Spanish EVENTUALMENTE and Portuguese EVENTUALMENTE both mean 'possibly, occasionally, perhaps' -- the opposite of a promise. Define FALSE FRIEND in-context as a word in one language that resembles a word in another but has a different meaning. T2: another canonical case -- English ACTUALLY means 'in fact, in reality' (I actually finished it yesterday). Spanish ACTUALMENTE and French ACTUELLEMENT both mean 'currently, at the present time' -- a different concept altogether. Identify what the false-friend cognate means in the other language. T3: the German-English pair GIFT. In English, a GIFT is a present. In German, GIFT means POISON (as in Giftschrank, poison-cabinet). The Germanic root is the same but the two branches diverged. This is a favourite alarm-bell example in language-textbooks. T4: more pairs -- EMBARRASSED (English: ashamed) vs EMBARAZADA (Spanish: pregnant); LIBRARY (English) vs LIBRAIRIE (French: bookshop, not library -- which is BIBLIOTHEQUE); SENSIBLE (English: practical) vs SENSIBLE (French/Spanish: sensitive). Identify which of four cross-language word pairs is a false friend. T5: distinguish FALSE FRIENDS (look alike, mean different) from TRUE COGNATES (look alike, mean similar -- FAMILY / FAMILIA / FAMILLE) and from PARTIAL COGNATES (overlap partially: English CHEF means head cook; French CHEF means the boss of anything, including a cook). Given four cross-language pairs, categorize each. Bryson's 'Mother Tongue' (1990) has a chapter on this in the English-loans-and-borrowings context.
source: PRIMARY: Oxford English Dictionary and Real Academia Espanola (RAE) for the eventually/eventualmente and actually/actualmente pairs; Duden dictionary for German GIFT (Gift, das) = poison. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'False friend' (browser, 2026-09-05) for the term, the standard example list (eventually/eventualmente, gift/Gift, embarrassed/embarazada, sensible/sensible), and the true-cognate/partial-cognate contrast. Bill Bryson, 'Mother Tongue' (1990) for the wider Germanic-and-Romance borrowing context. Steven Pinker, 'The Language Instinct' (1994) for the cross-language semantics framework.
framing_note: Etymology + register topic. Vocab-teaching invariant at T1: define FALSE FRIEND inline; T5 defines TRUE COGNATE and PARTIAL COGNATE. Punchline via the alarm-bell reveal (GIFT in German is POISON). Kid-safe throughout (embarazada/embarrassed is a classic textbook example, not crude). ACCURACY RAIL: every cross-language claim is drawn from standard reference dictionaries. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: give the English word and its cognate, ask what the cognate really means. DISTRACTOR POOL: true cognate, partial cognate, loanword, calque.
